newsitem.title: JAPAN: China likely to cut '97 grain imports.
newsitem.headline: China likely to cut '97 grain imports.

text.p: China is likely to cut grain imports this year substantially, especially wheat and corn, due to good harvests over the last two years, a senior official of the Chinese Agriculture Ministry said.
Gan Zuofu, deputy director general of Chinese Agriculture Ministry's international cooperation department, said China would import some grains this year to adjust local supply/demand problems.
"We had good grain harvests in the last two years and still hold ample stockpiles," Gan told Reuters late Monday evening.
"Some imports will be done moderately this year to adjust local supply/demand. But our basic policy is maintaining self sufficiency," he said in an interview.
China has reported two consecutive record grain harvests of 465 million tonnes in 1995 and 490 million tonnes last year.
Its corn imports for the first quarter of this year were zero, compared with 400,000 tonnes in the first two months of 1996, Chinese custom figures showed.
Wheat imports are also falling sharply. China imported 350,000 tonnes of wheat in the January-March period of this year, down 76.9 percent from a year earlier, it said.
Gan said that a key problem of Chinese agriculture was how to improve the grain distribution, citing high delivery costs from the grain-rich northeastern provinces to southern regions.

"Given the delivery cost between producing and consuming areas, it sometimes makes economic sense to export grain to other countries," he said. But he did not say how much grain exports would rise this year.
Chinese corn exports surged to 240,000 tonnes in the first quarter of this year, up 36,000 percent from the year-ago period when corn exports were effectively banned amid soaring domestic prices.
Rice exports in the first quarter rose to 80,000 tonnes, up 138.8 percent from the year-earlier period.
Gan also said China was under growing pressure from U.S. farmers groups to buy more grain.

"Some U.S. farmers' groups are pressuring us to import more grains because of the increasing population and food demand. But we're still able to produce enough grain to meet domestic demand," Gan said.
Gan is visiting Japan this week with Chinese Agriculture Minister Liu Jiang.
